H.name: Hydrogen
H.desc: The lightest element and the most abundant one in the universe.

He.name: Helium
He.desc: A light, unreactive gas used in balloons and for cooling.

Li.name: Lithium
Li.desc: The lightest metal and the key material in rechargeable batteries.

Be.name: Beryllium
Be.desc: A light, stiff metal used in aerospace components.

B.name: Boron
B.desc: Used in glass and detergents, and as a doping element in semiconductors.

C.name: Carbon
C.desc: The backbone element of living things; it forms chains that build countless compounds.

N.name: Nitrogen
N.desc: It makes up about 78 percent of the air and is the raw material of proteins and fertilisers.

O.name: Oxygen
O.desc: Used in respiration and combustion, and the most abundant element in the crust.

F.name: Fluorine
F.desc: The most reactive element, used in toothpaste and coatings.

Ne.name: Neon
Ne.desc: An unreactive gas that glows red when a current passes through it.

Na.name: Sodium
Na.desc: A metal that reacts violently with water and is one component of table salt.

Mg.name: Magnesium
Mg.desc: A light metal that sits at the centre of chlorophyll.

Al.name: Aluminium
Al.desc: A metal that is light and rust-free, used in cans and window frames.

Si.name: Silicon
Si.desc: The main constituent of sand and glass, and the material of semiconductor chips.

P.name: Phosphorus
P.desc: Used to store energy in cells and to build bone.

S.name: Sulfur
S.desc: Found as yellow crystals in volcanic areas and used to make sulfuric acid.

Cl.name: Chlorine
Cl.desc: A gas used for disinfection and the other component of table salt.

Ar.name: Argon
Ar.desc: The third most abundant gas in the air; being unreactive, it is used in welding.

K.name: Potassium
K.desc: A metal essential for nerves and muscles to work.

Ca.name: Calcium
Ca.desc: It builds bone and seashells and is the main constituent of limestone.

Sc.name: Scandium
Sc.desc: Light yet strong, used in bicycle and aerospace alloys.

Ti.name: Titanium
Ti.desc: Light and corrosion-free, used in implants and aircraft.

V.name: Vanadium
V.desc: A metal that makes steel far harder when alloyed into it.

Cr.name: Chromium
Cr.desc: It gives a rust-free shine and is used for plating.

Mn.name: Manganese
Mn.desc: It toughens steel and also goes into dry cells.

Fe.name: Iron
Fe.desc: The most widely used metal; it carries oxygen in the blood.

Co.name: Cobalt
Co.desc: A metal used in blue pigments and rechargeable battery electrodes.

Ni.name: Nickel
Ni.desc: Rust-free, so it goes into coins and stainless steel.

Cu.name: Copper
Cu.desc: A reddish metal used in wiring because it conducts electricity well.

Zn.name: Zinc
Zn.desc: Used in plating that keeps iron from rusting, and essential to the body.

Ga.name: Gallium
Ga.desc: Its melting point is so low that it melts in your hand; it is used in light-emitting devices.

Ge.name: Germanium
Ge.desc: The material of early semiconductors, now used in optical fibres.

As.name: Arsenic
As.desc: Highly toxic, yet also used as a semiconductor material.

Se.name: Selenium
Se.desc: It conducts electricity well under light, so it was used in photocopiers.

Br.name: Bromine
Br.desc: A rare element that is liquid at room temperature and reddish brown.

Kr.name: Krypton
Kr.desc: An unreactive gas used to fill high-performance light bulbs.

Rb.name: Rubidium
Rb.desc: It burns red in a flame test and is used in atomic clocks.

Sr.name: Strontium
Sr.desc: The metal that gives fireworks their red colour.

Y.name: Yttrium
Y.desc: A metal used in phosphors and superconductor materials.

Zr.name: Zirconium
Zr.desc: Resistant to heat and corrosion, so it is used in reactor components.

Nb.name: Niobium
Nb.desc: A metal used in superconducting magnets and strong alloys.

Mo.name: Molybdenum
Mo.desc: It withstands high temperatures, so it is alloyed into tool steel.

Tc.name: Technetium
Tc.desc: The first artificial element, almost absent in nature, used in medical imaging.

Ru.name: Ruthenium
Ru.desc: A precious metal used in electrical contacts and catalysts.

Rh.name: Rhodium
Rh.desc: Used in the catalysts that clean up car exhaust.

Pd.name: Palladium
Pd.desc: It absorbs hydrogen readily and is used in catalytic converters.

Ag.name: Silver
Ag.desc: It conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.

Cd.name: Cadmium
Cd.desc: Toxic, and once used as a rechargeable battery electrode.

In.name: Indium
In.desc: Used to make the transparent electrodes of touchscreens.

Sn.name: Tin
Sn.desc: It melts easily, so it is used in solder, and it is one component of bronze.

Sb.name: Antimony
Sb.desc: Used in flame retardants that keep things from burning.

Te.name: Tellurium
Te.desc: A metalloid used in solar cells and alloys.

I.name: Iodine
I.desc: Essential to thyroid hormones and used in antiseptics.

Xe.name: Xenon
Xe.desc: It gives a bright light, used in car headlamps and flash lamps.

Cs.name: Caesium
Cs.desc: One of the softest metals and the reference for atomic clocks.

Ba.name: Barium
Ba.desc: It blocks X-rays well, so it is used as a contrast agent.

La.name: Lanthanum
La.desc: Used in camera lens glass and rechargeable batteries.

Ce.name: Cerium
Ce.desc: The most abundant rare earth, used in polishes and catalysts.

Pr.name: Praseodymium
Pr.desc: Used in strong magnets and in welding goggle glass.

Nd.name: Neodymium
Nd.desc: The element behind the strongest permanent magnets.

Pm.name: Promethium
Pm.desc: A radioactive element that is almost absent in nature.

Sm.name: Samarium
Sm.desc: Used in magnets that keep their magnetism even at high temperatures.

Eu.name: Europium
Eu.desc: Used in banknote anti-counterfeiting and in red display phosphors.

Gd.name: Gadolinium
Gd.desc: The element used in magnetic resonance imaging contrast agents.

Tb.name: Terbium
Tb.desc: Used in green phosphors and magnetostrictive devices.

Dy.name: Dysprosium
Dy.desc: It helps magnets keep their strength at high temperatures.

Ho.name: Holmium
Ho.desc: It concentrates magnetic fields well and is used in powerful magnets.

Er.name: Erbium
Er.desc: Used to amplify signals in optical fibre communication.

Tm.name: Thulium
Tm.desc: A rare element used in portable X-ray devices.

Yb.name: Ytterbium
Yb.desc: Used in atomic clocks and fibre lasers.

Lu.name: Lutetium
Lu.desc: Used in petroleum refining catalysts and medical imaging.

Hf.name: Hafnium
Hf.desc: It absorbs neutrons well, so it is used in reactor control rods.

Ta.name: Tantalum
Ta.desc: Corrosion-resistant, so it is used in the capacitors of electronic components.

W.name: Tungsten
W.desc: It has the highest melting point of any metal, so it was used in bulb filaments.

Re.name: Rhenium
Re.desc: A rare metal used in the high-temperature parts of jet engines.

Os.name: Osmium
Os.desc: The densest element, and extremely hard.

Ir.name: Iridium
Ir.desc: The most corrosion-resistant metal, used in spark plugs.

Pt.name: Platinum
Pt.desc: Unreactive, so it is used widely in jewellery and catalysts.

Au.name: Gold
Au.desc: Its unchanging lustre made it money, and it is used in electrical contacts.

Hg.name: Mercury
Hg.desc: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and it is toxic.

Tl.name: Thallium
Tl.desc: Extremely toxic, and used in infrared equipment.

Pb.name: Lead
Pb.desc: A heavy, soft metal that blocks radiation well.

Bi.name: Bismuth
Bi.desc: A heavy element that is nonetheless low in toxicity, so it is used in medicines.

Po.name: Polonium
Po.desc: An element that emits strong radiation, discovered by the Curies.

Rn.name: Radon
Rn.desc: A radioactive gas that seeps out of the ground.

Fr.name: Francium
Fr.desc: The most reactive metal, but it decays almost immediately.

Ra.name: Radium
Ra.desc: It glows in the dark, and was discovered by the Curies.

Ac.name: Actinium
Ac.desc: The first element of the actinides; it emits strong radiation.

Th.name: Thorium
Th.desc: A radioactive metal studied as a reactor fuel.

Pa.name: Protactinium
Pa.desc: A rare radioactive element formed as uranium decays.

U.name: Uranium
U.desc: It undergoes fission and serves as the fuel of nuclear power.

Np.name: Neptunium
Np.desc: The first artificial element beyond uranium.

Pu.name: Plutonium
Pu.desc: Used as nuclear fuel and to power space probes.

Am.name: Americium
Am.desc: A tiny amount goes into smoke detectors.

Cm.name: Curium
Cm.desc: An artificial radioactive element named after the Curies.

Bk.name: Berkelium
Bk.desc: An artificial element made at Berkeley.

Cf.name: Californium
Cf.desc: It emits many neutrons, so it is used in survey instruments.

Es.name: Einsteinium
Es.desc: First found in the debris of a hydrogen bomb test.

Fm.name: Fermium
Fm.desc: An artificial element named after the physicist Fermi.

Md.name: Mendelevium
Md.desc: Named after Mendeleev, who built the periodic table.

No.name: Nobelium
No.desc: An artificial radioactive element named after Nobel.

Lr.name: Lawrencium
Lr.desc: Named after Lawrence, who invented the particle accelerator.

Rf.name: Rutherfordium
Rf.desc: Named after Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus.

Db.name: Dubnium
Db.desc: An element named after the Dubna laboratory in Russia.

Sg.name: Seaborgium
Sg.desc: Named after Seaborg, who created many artificial elements.

Bh.name: Bohrium
Bh.desc: Named after Bohr, who built the model of the atom.

Hs.name: Hassium
Hs.desc: An artificial element named after the German state of Hesse.

Mt.name: Meitnerium
Mt.desc: Named after Meitner, who explained nuclear fission.

Ds.name: Darmstadtium
Ds.desc: An element made in Darmstadt, Germany.

Rg.name: Roentgenium
Rg.desc: Named after Roentgen, who discovered X-rays.

Nh.name: Nihonium
Nh.desc: An element made in Japan; its name means Japan.

Fl.name: Flerovium
Fl.desc: Named after the Russian physicist Flerov.

Mc.name: Moscovium
Mc.desc: Named after the Moscow region of Russia.

Lv.name: Livermorium
Lv.desc: Named after the Livermore laboratory in the United States.

Ts.name: Tennessine
Ts.desc: An artificial element named after the US state of Tennessee.

Og.name: Oganesson
Og.desc: The element with the highest atomic number in the periodic table.
